hints: Start with the easiest cell to spot. Which of the three cells has to carry water in a fast, continuous column and also help hold the plant upright?
Now think about the phloem pair. Which one does all the metabolic work and loading, so needs lots of connections, and which one is the actual pipeline that needs a clear lumen?
walkthrough:
**Start with the xylem vessel element**

Think about its job first, it transports water and mineral ions up the plant in the transpiration stream.

To do this it is dead at maturity with no cytoplasm, no end walls and empty lumens, so water flows freely. Its walls are also strong and lignified for support and to resist collapse.

**Sort out the phloem sieve tube element**

Its job is to transport sucrose and other assimilates by mass flow.

It has no nucleus and only a thin layer of cytoplasm pushed to the edge. This reduces resistance to flow and leaves a clear pathway for sap.

**Check the companion cell**

The sieve tube cannot live alone, so the companion cell does the living work for it.

It is full of mitochondria for ATP to load sucrose, and it is linked to the sieve tube by many plasmodesmata for rapid communication and exchange. That combination matches row C perfectly.

options.A: All three descriptions are in the wrong columns. Thin cytoplasm belongs to the sieve tube, lignified walls belong to the xylem, and plasmodesmata belong to the companion cell.
options.B: Only the xylem description is correct here. Companion cells are living and full of organelles, not empty, and plasmodesmata are a companion cell feature, not a sieve tube feature.
options.C: Correct. Companion cell has many plasmodesmata, sieve tube has thin cytoplasm to reduce resistance, and xylem vessel is empty to allow free water flow.
options.D: All three are mismatched. Lignified walls are for xylem support, empty cells for water flow are xylem not phloem, and thin cytoplasm is for sieve tubes not xylem.
